Figure 1:Metrics often score a simple edit or a repeatedly generated copy above the enhancement chosen by people.Each row block shows one UIEB[29]photo: the raw image, the reference enhancement chosen by UIEB’s volunteers (green frame), one saturate, sharpen and CLAHE[71]edit at moderate strength (S+S+C), a milder S+S+C step applied 20 times (a condition people reject in our study,Sec.5), and the last frame of the four Nano Banana chains ofSec.6.
Below each photo are the scores of eight metrics, two per group: the default checkpoints with the highest and the lowest mean within-sceneκ\kappawith people in that group (Sec.4).↑\uparrow: a higher score means better quality, for all eight metrics.
Cell shade: rank of the panel among the eight for that metric, darkest and bold for the highest.
We show the three of the 20 drift photos in which a non-reference panel outscores the reference most often (30, 28, 24 of 56 comparisons).
Over all 20 photos, the rate is 30%, and 39% for the single S+S+C edit.Sections4,5and6measure these failures on full datasets.

Figure 2:Agreement with people is low on every reference, and no metric performs well on all five.Within-sceneκ\kappa(Sec.3.3) of the eight metrics ofFig.1, sorted by their worst value over the five references (last column). Blue: agreement, red: the metric prefers the image people liked less. Solid frame: the metric’s own training set. Dashed frame: a set from the same lab. Bottom rows: median and best value over all 73 metrics per reference (72 have all five values). The best values on UID2021[20]and SAUD[23]come from metrics evaluated on their own training data. All metrics with their 95% intervals are listed in the appendix.
